transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-06
Start time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Liu (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Aisha N'Dour (Redwood SE), Evan Morris (CedarPoint SRE), Priya Kapoor (CedarPoint Platform Eng), Carlos Ruiz (CedarPoint Security)

Summary (auto):
Quick demo/walkthrough of Redwood Console observability for inference: request playback, tracing heatmaps, error analysis, and fallbacks. Customer is evaluating hosted + private (VPC) options; main concerns are PII handling, KMS integration, and predictable p99 latency for 256-token responses. Action items and benchmarking agreed.

Topics covered:
- Request-level playback and filtering
- KV cache visibility and prefix cache hit rates (audio: K-V cash sometimes transcribed)
- Fallback policies and model variant routing
- Security/PII: KMS, audit logs, retention windows
- Benchmark plan and sample data requirements

[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): ok hey everyone thanks for carving time, this is Jordan from Redwood, Aisha and Samira here with me, we'll run through the observability playbook for inference and specifically show the request playback and trace flows. just to set expectations this is a demo-ish walkthrough not a deep infra scoping, though we can pivot to that.

[00:18] Evan (CedarPoint): great, yeah thanks. we're trying to understand how we could diagnose intermittent tail latency and also prove we won't leak customer PII when we send data to a hosted endpoint.

[00:28] Samira (Redwood SE): totally. we'll show the console traces, how to map requests to model versions, and then the error analysis workflow. we'll also call out the security controls — audit logs and KMS integration.

[00:45] Priya (CedarPoint): quick ask — can you show how we correlate a user request in our logs to the token-level timeline in Redwood? that's important for our incident playbooks.

[00:57] Aisha (Redwood SE): yes we'll demo that. the request inspector has request IDs you can ingest into your sidecar, and we expose a trace link that shows request lifecycle: routing decision, cache hit/miss, kernel selection, and estimated cost. sometimes the transcription says kernel "selection" weirdly but it's the kernel path.

[01:20] Jordan: ok jumping into the console. first screen is the request table — you can filter by time, model, customer token, or request metadata. i'll search for a sample trace evan sent earlier.

[01:40] [Screen share noise]

[01:48] Samira: here's the trace. top shows time-series latency, downstream calls (if any), and a flame-graph of compute stages. note the KV cache row — we expose prefix hit rate and the exact cached key length. in your case, evan, i see a lot of partial prefix hits which explains variable tail latency.

[02:12] Evan: partial prefix hits — meaning sometimes it hits only the last n tokens? could that cause re-computation?

[02:20] Samira: yeah, if the prefix in cache is shorter than your request prefix the runtime replays the missing KV segments; that adds CPU and can push you into queued batches, which inflates p95/p99.

[02:34] Priya: ok that makes sense. can you show the request playback? i want to see token timings.

[02:40] Aisha: clicking into playback, you get a per-token timeline. this is useful for seeing micro-bursts. the playback attaches metadata: model variant, quantization profile, host, and whether it fell back to a cheaper quantized path. we occasionally see 'K-V cash' transcribed in older exports, ignore that.

[03:05] [00:03:05] Jordan: there's also a helpful compare mode — you can select two request IDs and get a side-by-side of token latencies, prompt differences, and which kernel path ran. it's great for regression investigations after model rollouts.

[03:28] Evan: speaking of rollouts — if we do a canary and see degraded latency, can we auto-fallback to previous model?

[03:35] Samira: yes, rollouts support automatic fallback by latency SLA or error rate thresholds. we wire that into smart routing so requests that would otherwise hit the canary are routed to stable if p99 exceeds your SLO for more than N minutes.

[03:53] Carlos (Security): on PII — where does the raw prompt live? is it persisted in plaintext? and can we elect to not store raw prompts at all?

[04:02] Aisha: good question. default retention keeps request payloads for 30 days for debugging, but you can configure masked retention: redact PII on ingest, or use a non-persistent mode where only token-level metrics are kept and raw text is never stored. we support customer-managed keys for encrypt-at-rest and KMS for key rollover.

[04:24] Carlos: and audit logs for admin actions? we need to know who retrieved a trace.

[04:29] Samira: audit logs are available as a separate export stream; they track trace access, console downloads, and API keys used. you can pipe them to your SIEM via our Kafka/S3 connectors.

[04:44] Evan: ok can we talk about the benchmark plan? we wanted to compare hosted vs dedicated vs private for our 256-token responses at p99 < 350ms if possible.

[04:55] Jordan: absolutely. for that we'd run an isolated 2-hour load test with your traffic shape. Samira will set up a benchmark with batching and KV cache warmup to reflect production. we'll run hosted first, then replicate on Dedicated with same model quantization, and optionally on a Private node if you want the on-prem footprint.

[05:18] Samira: when you share the request traces, include token distribution and request inter-arrival time — that helps set batch windows and predicts real p99. Evan, you mentioned you saw spikes around midnight UTC?

[05:30] Evan: yes, our partner integrations cause spikes when they sync. we've been throttling but want to understand how Redwood's prefix caching would behave under that pattern.

[05:40] Samira: good — we'll simulate a spike in the benchmark. we'll also test cold vs warm KV cache scenarios. in the console i'll show a cache heatmap — here's a visualization: hot prefixes vs cold prefixes and eviction rates.

[05:58] [05:58] Priya: can we drill into an eviction event? curious about TTL and how to tune it.

[06:06] Aisha: click the cache event, it shows recent puts, TTL, size, and reason for eviction (LRU/size/TTL). TTL is tunable per deployment; Dedicated and Private give you direct control. Hosted we offer recommended profiles but you can request custom policies for enterprise agreements.

[06:30] Evan: on network — if we go VPC peering, how do you handle egress and ingress? any sidecar required?

[06:38] Jordan: for VPC, we support private connectivity via AWS PrivateLink and customer-managed peering. no sidecar required for basic routing; we provide a lightweight connector if you want mutual TLS or stronger auth.

[06:50] Carlos: does the connector store request data locally ever?

[06:54] Samira: no, the connector streams requests to your private deployment or to the Redwood control plane per your config. for an air-gapped on-prem install, logs stay in your environment.

[07:04] [07:04] Evan: one of our ops folks asked about request tagging — we want to map requests to internal feature flags. can we propagate X-headers?

[07:10] Aisha: yes, any header or metadata you send can be indexed and used for filtering in the request table and for grouping in charts. we recommend an internal customer_id and feature flag tag.

[07:22] Jordan: small demo thing — i'll intentionally trigger an error by sending an oversized token count so you can see the error analysis page.

[07:32] [approx sound of a test request]

[07:35] Samira: ok here's the failed request — top shows error class (validation/oom/kernel-fail). we show stack traces from the runtime, suggestion links (increase max_tokens, change batching), and the rate of similar errors in the last 24 hours.

[07:50] Priya: are those runtime traces safe to share with our app devs? any secrets?

[07:56] Aisha: runtime traces are scrubbed of any session tokens and we mask fields flagged as PII automatically if you enable masking rules. you can also limit who in your org can see runtime traces via RBAC.

[08:10] Evan: curious about cost insights — can we get token-level cost breakdown by route and model?

[08:17] Jordan: yes, console shows token cost, compute cost, and an amortized per-request cost. you can also tag routes to get cost by feature. this is part of Redwood Optimize recommendations we can run on your workload to suggest quantization or batching.

[08:32] Carlos: any concerns about quantization and hallucination drift? if we convert to int4, how do we ensure quality?

[08:40] Samira: good point. Optimize couples quantization suggestions with evals. we run a small test suite (your prompts + reference responses) and surface ROUGE/BLEU/embedding-similarity regressions. if quality drops beyond your threshold we won't recommend that quantization.

[08:58] [08:58] Evan: ok back to traces — can we export a sequence of requests with tokens and timings for our on-call postmortem?

[09:05] Aisha: yes exports are available as JSONL with sensitivity flags. you can redact on export and we also support streaming exports to S3.

[09:15] Priya: show me an example of a postmortem workflow — how would we tie the console trace to our PagerDuty incident?

[09:22] Samira: you can attach request IDs to an incident; our Slack integration can post the trace snippet into a channel, or our PagerDuty integration can embed the trace link in the incident so responders have token timelines and cache state at hand.

[09:40] Evan: that's useful. are there throttles or rate limits on the playback endpoint? we might want to pull many traces during an incident.

[09:48] Jordan: playback endpoints have rate limits to protect the runtime. for enterprise customers we offer higher throughput allowances or a dedicated playback replica so you can replay many traces without affecting production inference.

[10:00] Carlos: last security question — how do you handle subpoenas or legal holds? i.e., if a user requests deletion, what is the data workflow?

[10:08] Aisha: we support data subject access and deletion requests: we can scrub or delete raw payloads and we retain only aggregated metrics if deletion is requested. we keep an audit trail of deletion actions for compliance.

[10:22] [10:22] Jordan: ok wrapping into the benchmark and next steps. samira will own the benchmark config; jordan will send SOC2 and architecture diagrams; evan will provide sample traces and traffic profile.

[10:36] Evan: timeline looks good. one more ask — can you include a scenario where caching leads to unfair token reuse across tenants? we need to ensure no cross-tenant data leakage via cache keys.

[10:47] Samira: yep — cache keys are namespaced by tenant and by model variant; we'll add a cache-isolation test in the benchmark.

[10:58] Priya: and we'll also need details on key management for Private vs Hosted.

[11:04] Jordan: noted. we'll include a KMS comparison doc.

[11:12] [11:12] Carlos: ok last operational nit — do you provide request sampling so we don't store everything?

[11:18] Aisha: yes, sampling rules are configurable. you can sample by route, customer, or random percentage. you can also do synchronous masking so sensitive fields never hit the control plane.

[11:30] Jordan: great — let's summarize next steps: Jordan to send security pack by 2026-05-08, Samira to run a 2-hour benchmark by 2026-05-13, Evan to share traces by 2026-05-10, and we'll reconvene after results.

[11:50] Evan: thanks all. demo was helpful — we like the playback and cache heatmap.

[11:56] Priya: yeah nice to see token-level timings.

[12:00] Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up shortly.

End of transcript.
